source.title: From Concepts to Components: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery in Transformers
source.authors: Jingtong Su; Julia Kempe; Karen Ullrich

record.tranche_reason: The authors interpret a qualitative intervention result as possible evidence that an SAE feature is coarse or polysemantic, qualifying the idea that such features act as clean semantic units.
record.gate_note: The study uses SAE feature vectors as concept definitions and discovers attention-head modules associated with them. Head counts, cosine-similarity visualizations, reasoning and safety benchmark results, and vision classification results do not test the stated superposition or dictionary-unit claims. The San Francisco intervention is the reported result relevant to the authors’ specific caveat about an SAE feature being coarse or polysemantic.
record.test_reason: The study uses released Gemma Scope SAE decoder vectors as concept vectors to find attention-head modules, then reports its own method's performance (module locations, SAMI effects, benchmark gains). It never measures whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical or monosemantic. The San Francisco remark is the authors' speculation about why an intervention on attention heads (not on the SAE feature) gave untruthful output. The off-target effect could equally come from the five-head module. It is not a test of V5 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the main conclusions. The authors conclude that concepts map to sparse attention-head modules (3–10 heads). They find these modules unchanged between Gemma-2-2B base and instruct models, which they take as support for the superficial alignment hypothesis. Single-scalar SAMI on the modules can erase or amplify concepts: jailbreaking on HarmBench, +1.6% on GSM8K, and target-label accuracy driven to 0% in a ViT. The San Francisco feature-splitting point is a speculative aside, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cosine similarity to attribute concepts to attention heads and scalar intervention on those heads; it does not use the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The SAMI intervention strength is selected or varied by concept and experiment; for this San Francisco example it is s = -1.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative SAMI on the 'San Francisco' head module in Gemma-2-2B-IT also disrupts recall of other California cities. The authors speculate the SAE feature may be coarse or polysemantic (feature splitting).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interventions on components aligned with an SAE feature have off-target semantic effects, possibly reflecting coarse SAE features.

record.problems: The relevant evidence is a single qualitative example. The authors frame the connection to feature splitting as speculation; they do not systematically measure SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly test the versions of the claim. Other qualitative SAE interventions, quantitative benchmark results, and module visualizations concern concept attribution or intervention performance rather than the stated superposition or dictionary-unit claims.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweeps or feature geometry.
No test of capacity pressure or feature importance.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Uses pre-trained SAEs but does not test feature spread across neurons or SAE recovery.
Completeness, stability, canonicality and monosemanticity of SAE features are not measured. The only remark is speculative, about one qualitative example.

record.verdict_notes: The FQuAD comparison (SAMI 1.66% vs best SAE steering 3.98% French responses) compares the study's own method with SAE steering, so it should not be a row for V5. Reclassified from T5/tests to T4/uses_without_test.

versions.untested_parts: Not tested whether sparse features outnumber dimensions, overlap as nearly orthogonal directions, or undergo sparsity-dependent geometric transitions.
Not tested whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Uses previously released SAE features but does not test whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers them.
The San Francisco intervention is discussed as possible evidence of a coarse or polysemantic feature. Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not systematically tested.
Does not test whether model features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: GEMMA-2-2B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Applied negative SAMI intervention (s = -1) to the attention-head module discovered for the “San Francisco” SAE feature.

conditions.value: Give me five cities in California.

rows.measure: Qualitative generation; whether suppressing the feature-associated module affects the target concept and related California geography.
rows.baseline: Without intervention, the response lists California cities including Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, Sacramento, and San Jose.
rows.value: With intervention, the response gives several non-California cities and includes an incorrect description of New York City.
rows.note: The authors say the intervention can disrupt both the named concept and related California geography, and speculate that the SAE feature may be coarse or polysemantic. This is a qualitative example, not a systematic test of SAE feature completeness or stability.
rows.check: The intervention scales five attention heads chosen by cosine similarity, not the SAE feature. Off-target errors (non-California cities) cannot separate a polysemantic SAE feature from an overbroad head module. The authors themselves say the module may be overcomplete. The evidence is one qualitative generation, and the link to feature splitting is stated as speculation, so the row cannot show V5's effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The intervention is associated with errors beyond the target concept, which the authors suggest may reflect a coarse or polysemantic SAE feature (r1).
